clue.text: An opportunist with taking ways

parts.note: taking ways sounds like charm, but here it means habitually taking things, as a stealthy petty criminal who slips in through an open door does

explanation.surface: A description of a charming person who seizes every chance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking ways' usually means winning manners; read literally, it is the habit of taking other people's property.
explanation.definitionFit: This kind of thief pilfers by stealth when a chance presents itself, an opportunist criminal.

clue.text: Disgust at having to return one article and use another

indicators.note: to return means this article is written backwards in this down answer

parts.note: an is the indefinite article
taken as written
a is another indefinite article

explanation.surface: Revulsion at having to send one item back and use a different one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to return' turns AN into NA; 'article' looks like a shop item but is grammatical.
explanation.definitionFit: Nausea is sickness, and figuratively strong revulsion or loathing.

clue.text: Loathing for a particular form

parts.note: a version is a particular form or variant of something

explanation.surface: Hating one specific shape or style.
explanation.definitionFit: An aversion is a strong dislike or repugnance.

clue.text: The jester's criterion

definitions.meaning: the possessive names the fool character who belongs to a Shakespeare comedy

explanation.surface: The fool's standard of judgement.
explanation.walkthrough: Touchstone is the clown in Shakespeare's As You Like It; the word also means a test of quality.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the name of Shakespeare's court fool in As You Like It, and a standard against which quality is judged.

clue.text: A South- European international leader in bare accommodation

indicators.note: leader means only the opening letter of international is taken
accommodation means the letters are adapted or arranged to fit a new shape

explanation.surface: A southern European world leader stays in spartan lodgings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'accommodation' rearranges I (from 'international leader'), IN and BARE; it looks like lodging but signals adjustment.
explanation.definitionFit: An Iberian is a native of the peninsula holding Spain and Portugal in south-west Europe.

clue.text: Growing concern

parts.note: plays on going concern, a thriving business, and reads it literally as a business whose concern is growing crops

explanation.surface: A worry that keeps getting bigger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concern' means business, and 'growing' is cultivation, not increasing.
explanation.definitionFit: An agricultural holding is an enterprise dedicated to raising crops and livestock.

clue.text: Beasts responsible for the present transport system

definitions.text: Beasts responsible for the present transport system

parts.words: Beasts responsible for the present transport system
parts.note: present looks like now, current, but means gifts: these animals pull the sleigh that delivers Christmas presents

explanation.surface: Animals blamed for today's travel network.
explanation.walkthrough: 'present' means a gift, not the current time.
explanation.definitionFit: Santa Claus's sleigh is pulled by these antlered Arctic deer when he delivers gifts.

clue.text: A man of great age note, and so well-set-up

parts.note: me is a variant of mi, a note in the sol-fa scale
thus means so, in that way

indicators.note: set-up means the word for well is turned upwards, read from bottom to top in this down answer

parts.note: hale means healthy, well

explanation.surface: An elderly man noted for being so fit and sturdy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'well-set-up' looks like an adjective for a sturdy man; 'set-up' turns HALE into ELAH.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical patriarch lived 969 years, the longest life in the Bible.

clue.text: Each one houses a bird

indicators.note: houses means the word for one holds the bird inside it

parts.note: an ace is the one on a die or playing card
pie is an old name for the magpie

explanation.surface: Every single one of something is home to a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: PIE, the magpie, is an old word solvers meet often in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean for every one individually, as in costing a pound apiece.

clue.text: Queued, it might appear, for peace

indicators.note: might appear says the letters of the words before it could show up in another arrangement

explanation.surface: Standing in line looks like a route to tranquillity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might appear' rearranges QUEUED and IT.
explanation.definitionFit: Quietude is a state of calm and stillness, a synonym of peace.

clue.text: The odd blow may well go to the head

definitions.text: may well go to the head

parts.note: rum is an old-fashioned British word for strange or odd
a punch is a blow with the fist

explanation.surface: A strange punch might well land on someone's head.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition describes the answer as something that may go to the head, i.e. make one tipsy; the head in the surface is the target of a blow.
explanation.definitionFit: A spirit-based mixed drink can quickly make a drinker giddy, which is what going to the head means.

clue.text: A little dress, a ripping piece of material

indicators.note: A little says only a small part of the following words is wanted, the letters run on across them

explanation.surface: A tiny dress made from a splendid bit of cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A little' signals the run inside 'dresS A RIpping'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Indian garment is a single long length of cloth draped around the body.

clue.text: Long partnership at the wicket — and the fielder's angle

parts.note: in cricket a stand is a long partnership between two batsmen
point is a cricket fielding position, square of the batsman on the off side

explanation.surface: A cricket commentary on a big partnership and a fieldsman's view.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a STAND is a long batting partnership and POINT a fielding position.
explanation.definitionFit: A standpoint is a viewpoint or perspective, a way of looking at a matter.

clue.text: Such tradesmen get no rest — it's a mistake

indicators.note: mistake says the letters of the preceding words have been wrongly ordered

explanation.surface: A complaint that shopkeepers are overworked without a break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mistake' rearranges NO REST and ITS A.
explanation.definitionFit: Stationers are shopkeepers who sell paper, pens and office supplies.

clue.text: Outline permission is put in order

indicators.note: is put in order says the letters of permission are rearranged into a new sequence

explanation.surface: Planning permission in principle is being sorted out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is put in order' rearranges PERMISSION.
explanation.definitionFit: An impression is a rough idea or sketch, a general outline of something.

clue.text: Joining a group of players on leave

parts.note: a band is a group of musicians, i.e. players

explanation.surface: Joining a band of musicians while on holiday from work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leave' looks like a holiday noun but is the verb defined.
explanation.definitionFit: To abandon something is to desert it or go away from it for good.

clue.text: Everybody turned to Edward, as intended

parts.note: all means everybody

indicators.note: turned means this little word is written the other way round

parts.note: taken as written
Ted is a familiar short form of Edward

explanation.surface: Everyone turned towards Edward, as planned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' makes TO into OT.
explanation.definitionFit: Allotted means assigned or set aside for a purpose, as something earmarked.

clue.text: Pop in a pair the Spanish wear

indicators.note: in means the word for father is placed inside the abbreviation for pair

parts.note: pop and pa are both informal words for father
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: Slip into a pair of Spanish-style clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop in' looks like an instruction to put clothes on; Pop is father, PA.
explanation.definitionFit: Apparel is clothing, what one wears, used as a noun.

clue.text: Church member is first to come over bearing a seat

indicators.note: says the member comes first, ahead of the church, when the clue's pair is assembled

parts.note: an arm is a limb, a member of the body
an air is a manner or bearing

explanation.surface: A church member comes over first, carrying a chair.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a churchgoer arriving with a chair; the order instruction means the clue's two opening words are assembled back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: An armchair is a comfortable chair with side supports for the arms.

clue.text: A flier may be in a flat spin

indicators.note: spin says the letters are whirled into a new order

explanation.surface: A bird might be in a panic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a flat spin' is British for in a panic; 'spin' rearranges IN A FLAT.
explanation.definitionFit: The fantail is a breed of pigeon with a fan-shaped tail, a bird that flies.

clue.text: Measured study

explanation.surface: A careful, calculated piece of research.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it means slow and careful, as measured steps are; as a verb it means to think over or consider at length.

clue.text: Flyer with a taste for clothes

definitions.text: Flyer with a taste for clothes

parts.words: Flyer with a taste for clothes
parts.note: reads like a fashion-conscious airman, but describes a winged insect whose larvae literally eat woollen garments

explanation.surface: A pilot who loves fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taste' is literal: the larvae chew holes in wool.
explanation.definitionFit: The clothes variety of this insect has grubs that feed on fabric in wardrobes.

clue.text: Boys beat it!

parts.note: Tom is a boy's name, and the plural gives two of them
Tom is a boy's name, and the plural gives two of them

explanation.surface: Telling lads to clear off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beat it' looks like slang for go away, but means something you beat: a drum.
explanation.definitionFit: A tom-tom is a hand-beaten drum, the object one strikes.

clue.text: Openly striking Tories

parts.note: workers out are on strike
the Tories, Britain's Conservative Party, are the political right

explanation.surface: Conservatives are openly on strike.
explanation.walkthrough: TORIES are members of the UK Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: Outright means frankly and without reserve, as in saying something straight out.

clue.text: Have to struggle for breath, so talk softly

parts.note: gas is idle chatter or talk
p is piano, the musical direction for softly

explanation.surface: Being breathless, one has to speak quietly.
explanation.definitionFit: To gasp is to pant or inhale sharply when short of air.

clue.text: One can't separate the beer and port

indicators.note: separate means the beer is split apart with the other letters sitting between its parts

parts.note: ale is a type of beer
I is the Roman numeral for one
taken as written without its apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone unable to keep the beer apart from the fortified wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'port' looks like the drink beside the beer; it is a harbour city in Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: Alicante is a Mediterranean seaport city in south-east Spain.

clue.text: Relations see the point in polite society.

indicators.note: in means the compass point goes inside the word for polite

parts.note: nice can mean well-mannered or polite
E, east, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: Family members get the joke among well-mannered company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'see the point' looks like an idiom for understanding; 'see' is a link and 'the point' is E.
explanation.definitionFit: Nieces are relatives, the daughters of one's brothers or sisters.

clue.text: Characters quite unaffected by any reversal

definitions.text: Characters quite unaffected by any reversal

parts.words: Characters quite unaffected by any reversal
parts.note: sounds like people who stay calm whatever misfortune strikes, but describes a string of letters that reads the same backwards

explanation.surface: People who remain unshaken whatever setbacks befall them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' means letters, not people, and 'reversal' is reading them backwards, not a setback.
explanation.definitionFit: A word or phrase like 'level' or 'madam' reads identically in both directions.
